attempts.response: {"title":"A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12","authors":"Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris","field_subfield":"Materials Science / Computational Chemistry (Solid-State Ionics)","type_of_paper":"Methodology + Applied Computational Study (preprint)","executive_summary":"Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidate materials, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its superior interfacial stability against metallic Li, yet it is not stable at room temperature and must be stabilised with substitutional dopants. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h crystallographic sites, and there is no consensus in the literature about the correct 24d :96h Li occupancy. Because many computational studies begin from an assumed experimental occupancy to build an idealised unit cell, the authors argue that without knowing whether those starting structures are near the ground state, downstream thermodynamic and observable properties may be poorly described. To address this, the authors present a combinatorial workflow that enumerates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and ranks them energetically. They first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets — the 200 lowest-energy structures from the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random sample of ~1000 structures — and fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model using a frequency list of all Li-Li interactions as descriptors. The MLR achieves a test-set correlation of 0.9996 and finds that all structures lie within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. The 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 8:48 ratio, with the 19th lowest being 9:47, and four 8:48 structures lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the global minimum. Geometry optimisation of these four structures narrows the energy gap further, with the lowest-energy structure (label 1095859) being 0.58 eV lower than the geometry-optimised lowest single-point structure after a 96h to 24d transition changing the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may describe structures that are not physically feasible or stable, and they release all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not include a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.executive_summary: Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidate materials, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its superior interfacial stability against metallic Li, yet it is not stable at room temperature and must be stabilised with substitutional dopants. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h crystallographic sites, and there is no consensus in the literature about the correct 24d :96h Li occupancy. Because many computational studies begin from an assumed experimental occupancy to build an idealised unit cell, the authors argue that without knowing whether those starting structures are near the ground state, downstream thermodynamic and observable properties may be poorly described. To address this, the authors present a combinatorial workflow that enumerates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and ranks them energetically. They first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets — the 200 lowest-energy structures from the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random sample of ~1000 structures — and fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model using a frequency list of all Li-Li interactions as descriptors. The MLR achieves a test-set correlation of 0.9996 and finds that all structures lie within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. The 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 8:48 ratio, with the 19th lowest being 9:47, and four 8:48 structures lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the global minimum. Geometry optimisation of these four structures narrows the energy gap further, with the lowest-energy structure (label 1095859) being 0.58 eV lower than the geometry-optimised lowest single-point structure after a 96h to 24d transition changing the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may describe structures that are not physically feasible or stable, and they release all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not include a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. Notable omissions include the absence of author affiliations, funding statements, and explicit hyperparameter details beyond the DFT settings, which are recorded under the relevant fields.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidate materials, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its superior interfacial stability against metallic Li, yet it is not stable at room temperature and must be stabilised with substitutional dopants. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h crystallographic sites, and there is no consensus in the literature about the correct 24d :96h Li occupancy. To address this, the authors present a combinatorial workflow that enumerates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and ranks them energetically. They first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets — the 200 lowest-energy structures from the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random sample of ~1000 structures — and fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model using a frequency list of all Li-Li interactions as descriptors. The MLR achieves a test-set correlation of 0.9996 and finds that all structures lie within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. The 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 8:48 ratio, with the 19th lowest being 9:47, and four 8:48 structures lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the global minimum. Geometry optimisation of these four structures narrows the energy gap further, with the lowest-energy structure (label 1095859) being 0.58 eV lower than the geometry-optimised lowest single-point structure after a 96h to 24d transition changing the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may describe structures that are not physically feasible or stable, and they release all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not include a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. Notable omissions include the absence of author affiliations, funding statements, and explicit hyperparameter details beyond the DFT settings, which are recorded under the relevant fields.

Research Context
The motivation is that solid electrolytes offer higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs versus liquid electrolytes. A key challenge is electrochemical and chemomechanical stability, with dendrite formation causing short-circuits even in the most stable solid electrolytes. c-LLZO is highlighted as having the best interfacial stability of popular fast ion conductors against metallic Li, but it is not stable at room temperature and requires dopants. c-LLZO has a Li diffusivity over two orders of magnitude smaller than the tetragonal phase, motivating interest in the cubic polymorph. There is no consensus in the literature about c-LLZO's Li occupancy, as shown in the summary of experimental and theoretical studies. Prior computational studies typically start from an experimental occupancy to build an idealised unit cell, which may not be near the ground state. Without knowing if structures are near the ground state, more complicated thermodynamic and observable properties may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to identify and rank all energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO for a crystallographically predicted structure. The authors hypothesise that imposing a minimal Li-Li distance eliminates physically infeasible structures with overlapping Li atoms. The authors hypothesise that removing symmetry images reduces the configuration space to unique conformations. The authors hypothesise that a machine learning-based energetic ordering can rank the remaining structures efficiently. The authors hypothesise that the 24d :96h ratio is indicative of a structure's energy, with lower energy structures avoiding 24d occupation. The authors predict that a large portion of previously reported structures may not be feasible or stable. The authors predict that the workflow can be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO), which has the space group Ia 3d with Li partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites. The 24d site is tetrahedral, and the 96h site occurs at a tetrahedral/octahedral interface. The framework uses the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. as the basis for generating structures. The number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is approximately 7.4 × 10 34, rendering brute-force combinatorial enumeration unviable. The authors neglect the 48g site because it is not reported in most refinements found in the literature. The authors impose a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å to eliminate overlapping Li atoms. This cutoff is less than 2 times the ionic radius of a Li atom and smaller than the minimum distance in t-LLZO (2.56 Å). The geometric constraint limits 24d :96h ratios, with a maximum of 48 out of 96h sites occupied at any time. Each 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites because they are within 1.67 Å of this site. The total number of structures for each 24d :96h ratio is given in Table 1, with the total for the stoichiometric case calculated as x tot. Generating all allowed structures yields approximately 2.3 × 10 8 structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. To reduce memory, the authors construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure. The connectivity matrix is defined as the distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom, then flattened and sorted. The authors use local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches, reducing pairwise comparison from O(N 2 ) to O(N ). LSH is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions, and the method's high specificity is a trade-off. Symmetry reduction yields approximately 1% symmetrically unique structures, reducing the space by a factor of ~100. After symmetry reduction, the configuration space is around 2 × 10 6 structures, enabling energetic ordering. The authors perform DFT calculations on two subsets: the 200 lowest-energy structures from COMPASSIII and a random sample of ~1000 structures. In total, 1235 single-point DFT calculations were performed. All DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code, which scales linearly with the number of atoms versus cubic scaling in conventional DFT. The authors use the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional with a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The authors assume the base LaZrO structure remains relatively unchanged, so energetic changes are primarily due to Li placement. Structures are represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions as descriptors for the MLR model. The data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio. The COMPASSIII forcefield was applied to only the Li-sublattice, ordering the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991. The authors use CASTEP on-the-fly generated pseudopotentials for the ONETEP calculations. The authors use the atomic simulation environment (ASE) python package's symmetry equivalence check to validate the LSH method on the 12:44 and 13:43 ratios. The authors perform 20 geometry optimisation calculations using BFGS, with site transitions listed in order of frequency. The authors note that the energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. The authors tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. The authors neglect entropic contributions and assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which are both approximations.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow begins by eliminating structures with overlapping Li atoms based on nearest-neighbour counts. The authors generate all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy, eliminating directly neighbouring 96h sites. The authors then populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously. The authors use the Buschmann et al. framework to generate all possible structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. The authors construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice to reduce structures to unique conformations. The connectivity matrix is flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity across all matrices. The authors use LSH to perform fast approximate similarity searches, reducing memory requirements. The authors validate the LSH method against more rigorous methods, using ASE's symmetry equivalence check on the two smallest ratios. The authors assign new space groups for all 2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures and plot the order of the group against the MLR energy. The authors test including the symmetry of the structure in the MLR model and find it makes a negligible difference. The authors perform DFT calculations on the 200 lowest-energy structures from COMPASSIII and a random sample of ~1000 structures. The authors fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model to the DFT energies using the Li-Li interaction frequency list. The authors apply the MLR model to the test set to evaluate predictive performance. The authors perform geometry optimisation calculations on the final four structures to assess the effect of relaxation. The authors find that the 96h to 24d transition yielded the lowest overall energy structure (label 1095859), 0.58 eV lower than the geometry-optimised lowest single-point structure. The authors use a 3rd order polynomial fit to the Li-dimer energy calculations to find the optimal inter-atomic distance. The authors perform 30 single-point calculations in a large unit cell to prevent self-interaction for the Li-dimer. The authors find the minimum energy of the Li-dimer likely occurs at approximately 2.7 Å.

Key Results
The MLR model achieves a test-set correlation of 0.9996, indicating excellent predictive performance. All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest energy structure. The 19 of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48, with the 19th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation. Four structures, all 8:48, lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates, all with the same 24d configuration. The geometry optimisation of the final four structures narrows the energy gap further. The lowest overall energy structure (label 1095859) is 0.58 eV lower than the geometry-optimised lowest single-point structure. The 96h to 24d transition changed the ratio of the structure from 9:47 to 10:46, the only time such a feature was observed. None of the site changes (96h to 96h, 96h to 48g, 96h to 24d) correlated significantly with the geometry-optimised energy. There is a negative correlation between the mean distance moved of all Li atoms and increasing energy of the final optimised structure. There is a weaker negative correlation between distance to a crystallographic site and energy. The COMPASSIII forcefield ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991. The COMPASSIII forcefield predicted a more pronounced separation of energies depending on the 24d :96h ratio than ONETEP. The Li-dimer minimum energy likely occurs at approximately 2.7 Å, with a large energy penalty for Li atoms approaching 1.7 Å. The most symmetric ratio appears to be 8:48, followed by 12:44 and 10:46, with a slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry. The Coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures, as shown in the supporting information.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results support the hypothesis that the 24d :96h ratio is indicative of a structure's energy, with lower energy structures avoiding 24d occupation. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates, all with the same 24d configuration, suggesting the 96h configuration is the primary determinant of energy. The negative correlation between Li atom movement and energy suggests that movement from original sites is preferable to attain lower energies. The slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry suggests symmetry may be a weak descriptor, though including it in the MLR made a negligible difference. The results imply that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may describe structures that are not physically feasible or stable. The workflow's ability to enumerate and rank all possible structures provides a foundation for improving accuracy and reproducibility in c-LLZO research. The method's extensibility to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals broadens its applicability beyond c-LLZO. The exclusion of non-Li elements in the COMPASSIII forcefield was deemed sufficient to energetically order structures, as the majority of energy differences come from unique Li configurations.

Contradictions And Limitations
The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions, which is a significant approximation for determining the ground state. The procedure assumes a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which is another approximation. The authors note that under the majority of theoretical schemes the 24d :96h ratio is likely not maintained after geometry relaxation, and the final ratio is rarely reported. The choice of initial structure in prior studies was mostly for convenience, and a low-energy structure is not necessarily guaranteed even with AIMD. The LSH method's high specificity is a trade-off for increased speed and lower memory costs, potentially limiting its accuracy. The COMPASSIII forcefield's more pronounced energy separation than ONETEP was considered too large to surmount, motivating the MLR model. The authors acknowledge that a large-scale energy prediction of the geometry-optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and has not been peer-reviewed, which may affect the reliability of the findings. The paper omits the exact values in Table 1 for the number of structures for each 24d :96h ratio, which are central to the configuration space analysis. The paper omits the exact value of x tot for the stoichiometric case, which is calculated in the text.

Claims
The workflow can identify and rank all energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO for a crystallographically predicted structure. The workflow presents a methodology to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO. The workflow generates all possible structures and orders them energetically. The MLR model achieves a test-set correlation of 0.9996. The workflow reduces the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 to ~2 × 10 6 structures. The workflow can be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions, which limits its ability to identify the true ground state. Data And Code Availability
The authors provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database. The structures are published alongside the results in the Supporting Information (SI) section. The authors do not explicitly state the URL or access method for the freely accessible database.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors validate the LSH method against more rigorous methods, using ASE's symmetry equivalence check on the 12:44 and 13:43 ratios. The authors tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. The authors test including the symmetry of the structure in the MLR model and find it makes a negligible difference. The COMPASSIII forcefield ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991, validating its use on the Li-sublattice. The authors note that any minimal distance between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable for a numerical implementation. The authors find that the Coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures.

Ethical Considerations
The paper is published under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license, which restricts commercial use and derivatives. The paper is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed, which may affect the reliability of the findings.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1b shows the c-LLZO structure with the 24d :96h ratios that cannot exist without a Li-Li interaction below the crystal ionic diameter. Figure 1c shows the range of predicted structures in the literature, indicating disagreement about the ground state. Figure 2b shows the ratio of the 20 lowest energy structures, with 19 of 20 having a ratio of 8:48. Three Takeaways
The core contribution is a workflow to identify and rank all energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO for a crystallographically predicted structure. The strongest evidence is the MLR model's test-set correlation of 0.9996, indicating excellent predictive performance. The future path is to extend the workflow to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals, and to release all generated structures in a freely accessible database.
